sections.h2: What is different about selling a house in Wheaton?
sections.html:
Wheaton adds a city transfer stamp to every sale, and the buyer pays for it. The city also wants the seller's final utility bill settled before the stamp is issued, so the two sides of a closing depend on each other. Wheaton is the DuPage County seat and sits about 25 miles west of Chicago, in Milton and Winfield Townships.

The same rules apply whether the house is listed, sold privately or bought for cash as-is. What changes is who files the stamp application and how early the final water reading is booked.

sections.h2: How much is the Wheaton real estate transfer stamp?
sections.html:
The stamp costs $2.50 per $1,000 of full consideration, taken from line 11 of the Illinois MyDec PTAX-203 declaration, with the price rounded to the nearest thousand. The buyer, called the grantee, buys it. On top of that, the state levies its own tax of 50 cents per $500 of declared value under 35 ILCS 200/31-10.

A buyer can get the stamp four ways, according to the city's Finance Department page:

  • Online through the transfer stamp portal, after creating an account.
  • By email to finance@wheaton.il.us.
  • By UPS or FedEx to the Finance Department at 303 W. Wesley St., Wheaton, IL 60187.
  • In person at City Hall, first floor.

Paper filings need a signed stamp application, a copy of the completed PTAX-203 or the deed, and a completed city utility account application form.

sections.h2: Which Wheaton transfers are exempt from the stamp tax?
sections.html:
Most Wheaton sales are non-exempt because they carry money. The city lists examples of exempt deeds, and the full list sits in City Code Chapter 66, Article VII, Section 66-190.

Common exemptions listed on the City of Wheaton transfer stamp page
Exempt situationNote
Transfer to or from a trustStill needs a $0 value stamp
Actual consideration under $100.00Same $0 stamp
Property acquired by or from a governmental bodyDocumentation required
Buyer sold a Wheaton primary home and is buying a new principal residence in WheatonExemption 13
Buyer is the natural or adopted child of a sellerExemption 14

An exempt stamp carries a $25 administrative fee and needs a signed, notarized deed. Since October 1, 2025 Wheaton no longer pays transfer tax refunds. Situations that once qualified for a refund are now handled as exemptions when the stamp is bought, so supporting documents must be ready on the closing timeline.

sections.h2: What must a Wheaton seller do before the stamp is issued?
sections.html:
The seller must call the city 5 to 7 days before closing to book a final water reading, at 630-260-2000 or waterbilling@wheaton.il.us. The final bill, or an estimate of it, then has to be paid in full. The city also checks for other unpaid charges.

  • Water, sanitary sewer and stormwater utility fees.
  • Inspection fees.
  • Building permit fees.
  • Property maintenance fines.

Because building permit fees and property maintenance fines are on the list, ask the city for a balance on your account a couple of weeks ahead and clear anything outstanding before the contract date.

sections.h2: What do Census numbers show for Wheaton housing?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau puts median home value at $455,700 for 2020 to 2024, with median gross rent of $1,799 and median household income of $120,008. About 71.7% of homes are lived in by their owners, across 19,588 households averaging 2.54 people.

  • The July 2025 estimate is 54,065 residents, essentially level with the 2020 count of 53,970.
  • Some 64.5% of adults 25 and older hold a bachelor's degree or more.
  • Monthly costs for owners average $2,764 with a mortgage and $1,138 without one.
  • Around 86.4% of residents had the same address a year earlier.

sections.h2: How do property taxes work for a Wheaton seller?
sections.html:
Wheaton parcels are billed by DuPage County. Taxes arrive a year behind, so the bills mailed April 29, 2026 covered tax year 2025 and carried June 1 and September 1 installments, both now past. The general homestead and senior exemptions are each $8,000 on the county's current notice, and a seller should confirm both appear on the bill. For assessed value questions, the county treasurer points owners to the local assessor's number printed on the bill.

On the settlement statement the title company divides the unpaid tax for the year. State law also requires sellers of one to four residential units to hand over a completed disclosure report before a contract is signed (765 ILCS 77/20). For a rough house, that report is where known problems get written down.

sections.h2: What can slow down a Wheaton closing?
sections.html:
Most delays come from the utility step or from a missing exemption record. The city is firm that the transfer stamp cannot be issued until the final utility bill is paid, so a late call to the utility office can hold up the stamp and the recording that follows.

  • Booking the final water reading later than the 5 to 7 day window the city requests.
  • Forgetting that the buyer, not the seller, submits the PTAX-203 copy and the utility account application.
  • Claiming an exemption without a notarized deed or supporting documents.
  • Leaving building permit fees or property maintenance fines unpaid.
  • Counting on a refund after closing, which the city no longer issues.

Sellers who need to leave quickly, such as an estate heir or an owner relocating for work, should line up these items with the title company the week the contract is signed.

sections.h2: What shaped Wheaton and its neighborhoods?
sections.html:
The Wheaton brothers came from Connecticut, Warren laid claim to land in the center of town in 1837, and the place became a village on February 24, 1859, then a city on April 24, 1890. It won the county seat vote in 1867 by 1,686 to 1,635, and the 1887 courthouse is listed as a historic landmark at the federal level. The county moved its court complex about two miles west in 1990, and downtown has since added condominium and business projects.

Land area totals 11.32 square miles, and the city has been landlocked for decades. Most of it lies in Community Unit School District 200, feeding Wheaton North and Wheaton Warrenville South high schools, while the northeast corner is in Glen Ellyn District 41 and one elementary school in the southeast belongs to District 89. Wheaton College sits just east of downtown, and the city's 2025 financial report lists the DuPage County Government Center, District 200 and Wheaton College among its largest employers. The Union Pacific West Line runs through downtown, where the 758-unit Wheaton Center apartment complex with its two twenty-story towers is a recognizable landmark. The DuPage County Fairgrounds are in Wheaton as well, and the downtown business association runs seasonal events that bring foot traffic past listings in the center of town.

faqs.q: Who pays the Wheaton transfer stamp, the buyer or the seller?
faqs.a: The buyer, also called the grantee, buys the stamp. The seller's job is to book the final water reading and pay the final utility bill, because the city will not issue the stamp until that bill is settled.

faqs.q: What is the Wheaton transfer stamp rate?
faqs.a: It is $2.50 per $1,000 of full consideration from line 11 of the PTAX-203, with the price rounded to the nearest thousand. Exempt deeds still need a $0 stamp and a $25 administrative fee.

faqs.q: How early should I schedule the final water reading in Wheaton?
faqs.a: Call 5 to 7 days before closing. The city's Finance Department takes requests at 630-260-2000 or waterbilling@wheaton.il.us, and the final bill must be paid before the stamp is issued.

faqs.q: Did Wheaton stop refunding transfer tax?
faqs.a: Yes, as of October 1, 2025. Buyers who would have qualified for a refund, such as a Wheaton homeowner moving to another Wheaton home or a child buying from a parent, now claim Exemption 13 or 14 when they apply for the stamp.

faqs.q: Which county handles property tax for Wheaton?
faqs.a: DuPage County. Its treasurer mails one bill with two installment coupons, and the 2025 bills were due June 1 and September 1, 2026. Both dates have passed, and the county bills a year in arrears.
